notes: Fixed slots 0,2,3,4,19,22 not written. Religious slots use real Northern bodies (Buddhist association, Archdiocese of Hanoi, Al-Noor mosque, Evangelical Church); slot 11 is a Catholic underground rooted in the 1956 Quynh Luu uprising. Hardliners (Le Duc Tho) in 6, Ministry of Public Security in 7, Pham Van Dong's Council of Ministers in 13, jailed 1967 'revisionists' in 18, Kim Ngoc's household contracting in 16.

1.name: Uy ban Lien lac Cong giao Yeu To quoc Yeu Hoa binh
1.english: Liaison Committee of Patriotic and Peace-Loving Catholics
1.native_full: Uy ban Lien lac nhung nguoi Cong giao Viet Nam yeu To quoc, yeu hoa binh
1.text:
The Liaison Committee of Patriotic and Peace-Loving Catholics was created in 1955 by the Workers' Party to organize the Catholics who stayed in the North after hundreds of thousands of their co-religionists fled south. Led by priests and laymen loyal to the regime, it sits in the Fatherland Front and speaks for the parishes of Nam Dinh, Ninh Binh and Phat Diem.

The committee preaches that a good Catholic is a good patriot: obedience to the state, work in the cooperatives and support for the war against the Americans, with loyalty to Rome confined to matters of faith. Its following is limited, but its leverage lies in being the only legal channel between the party and the Northern Catholic villages.

5.name: Luc luong Thanh nien Xung phong
5.native_full: Luc luong Thanh nien Xung phong
5.text:
The Youth Volunteer Force is the corps of young men and women mobilized by the Working Youth Union to serve behind and at the front: repairing roads, bridges and ferries under bombing, carrying supplies down the Truong Son trail and clearing unexploded ordnance. On 1 January 1970 tens of thousands serve in its brigades, many of them young women from the Red River Delta.

The volunteers embody the most radical spirit of the revolution: total sacrifice, egalitarian collective life and impatience with bureaucrats and comfort in the rear. They are fiercely committed to the war in the South and to Ho Chi Minh's memory, and their leverage lies in their indispensable labour on the supply routes and their moral prestige.

6.name: Phe Chong Xet lai
6.text:
Phe Chong Xet lai is the hardline faction in the Workers' Party leadership that crushed the so-called Revisionist Anti-Party Affair of 1967, when dozens of cadres accused of pro-Soviet, peaceful-coexistence views were jailed without trial. Its enforcer is Le Duc Tho, head of the party's Organization Department, backed by the security ministry and veteran ideologues.

The faction insists on Marxist-Leninist orthodoxy, iron party discipline, collectivized agriculture and war in the South until total victory, and denounces Khrushchevite revisionism and any soft compromise in Paris. It balances between Moscow and Peking without trusting either, and its leverage lies in control of cadre appointments and the purge files.

7.name: Bo Cong an
7.text:
The Ministry of Public Security is the North's police and intelligence apparatus, led since the early 1950s by Tran Quoc Hoan. It runs the People's Armed Security Forces, the border guards, the household registration system and a network of re-education camps for 'reactionaries', former officials of the old regime and suspected spies.

The ministry stands for vigilance against saboteurs and enemy agents, strict control over movement, religion and speech, and the mobilization of the rear for war. Trained with Soviet, East German and Chinese help, it answers to the Politburo, and its leverage lies in files on every family and the power to arrest anyone.

8.name: Hoi Phat giao Thong nhat Viet Nam
8.native_full: Hoi Phat giao Thong nhat Viet Nam
8.text:
The Unified Buddhist Association of Vietnam was formed in 1958 to bring the Northern pagodas and monks under a single body loyal to the Democratic Republic, with its seat at the Quan Su pagoda in Hanoi. Led by the venerable Thich Tri Do, it belongs to the Fatherland Front and sends delegations to Buddhist peace conferences abroad.

The association teaches that the dharma and socialism agree on compassion and justice, supports the war against the Americans and denounces the Saigon regime's treatment of Southern monks. It works for a modest revival of pagoda life under state supervision, and its leverage lies in the trust of village Buddhists and its usefulness to the party's diplomacy.

9.name: Tong Giao phan Ha Noi
9.text:
The Archdiocese of Hanoi is led by Archbishop Joseph Marie Trinh Nhu Khue, appointed in 1960 when Rome established the Vietnamese hierarchy, and is the spiritual centre of the Catholics who remained in the North. Its priests are few and aging, its seminaries restricted, and contacts with the Holy See pass through rare letters and visitors.

The archbishop and his clergy resist the party's efforts to subordinate the Church through the patriotic Catholic committee, defending the authority of Rome, the sacraments and the right to train priests. They avoid open politics, but their leverage lies in the deep loyalty of Catholic villages that obey the bishop before the cadre.

10.name: Thanh duong Hoi giao Al-Noor
10.native_full: Thanh duong Hoi giao Al-Noor Ha Noi
10.text:
The Al-Noor Mosque on Hang Luoc street, built in the 1890s by Indian Muslim traders under French rule, is the only mosque in Hanoi and the centre of the North's tiny Muslim community of South Asian, Malay and Arab descent. Most of its families left in 1954; on 1 January 1970 it serves a few dozen residents and the staff of Arab and Muslim embassies.

The congregation keeps to worship and avoids politics, thanking the government for its protection and joining religious delegations of the Fatherland Front when asked. Its leverage is diplomatic: friendship with Algeria, Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Indonesia gives Hanoi reason to keep the mosque open and its imam respected.

11.name: Quynh Luu
11.text:
Quynh Luu is the clandestine legacy of the November 1956 uprising in the Catholic villages of Quynh Luu in Nghe An, when peasants enraged by the land reform rose against the cadres and were crushed by army troops. In 1970 its heirs are a scattering of Catholic families, former prisoners and dismissed village elders in Nghe An and the delta, watched by the security police.

They pray for the fall of the atheist state, listen secretly to Saigon and Vatican radio and hope for deliverance from the South or from heaven. They are unarmed and leaderless, but their leverage lies in deep-rooted grievance: in a moment of crisis the parishes that rose once could rise again.

12.name: Hoi thanh Tin Lanh Viet Nam (Mien Bac)
12.native_full: Hoi thanh Tin Lanh Viet Nam (Mien Bac)
12.text:
The Evangelical Church of Vietnam (North) is the small Protestant church left in the Democratic Republic after the missionaries of the Christian and Missionary Alliance and most believers departed in 1954. Headquartered in Hanoi, it counts a few thousand members in the capital, Haiphong and the delta provinces, led by Vietnamese pastors under the eye of the Fatherland Front.

The church avoids confrontation, preaches personal faith and good citizenship and endorses the government's positions on the war, hoping in return to keep its chapels and its Bible printing. Its leverage is slight, resting on the tight discipline of its congregations and its ties to Protestant peace councils abroad.

13.name: Hoi dong Chinh phu
13.text:
The Council of Ministers is the government of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, headed since 1955 by Prime Minister Pham Van Dong, Ho Chi Minh's closest companion. Through the bombing years it directed the ministries, planning commissions and state enterprises that evacuated factories into the countryside and distributed Soviet and Chinese aid.

The council is the voice of administration and pragmatism: economic recovery after the 1968 bombing halt, careful planning, rational use of aid and diplomacy alongside war. Pham Van Dong commands respect abroad, and the council's leverage lies in the state machine, the planners and the technical cadres who must turn party slogans into rice, coal and electricity.

14.name: Khu tu tri Viet Bac
14.text:
The Viet Bac Autonomous Region, created in 1956, gives the Tay, Nung, Dao and other highland peoples of the northern provinces a measure of self-government in the old revolutionary base area where the Viet Minh sheltered in the 1940s. Its administration is staffed by minority cadres who fought beside Ho Chi Minh, and it holds a special place in party mythology.

Its leaders defend local customs, languages and land rights within socialism, ask for roads, schools and clinics, and are wary of lowland cadres and of Chinese influence across the border. Their leverage lies in strategic geography, the loyalty of the highlands and the prestige of the revolution's cradle.

15.name: Tu san Dan toc
15.text:
Tu san Dan toc names the remnants of the patriotic business class that backed the revolution in 1945, symbolized by Trinh Van Bo, the Hanoi textile merchant who gave his fortune to the Viet Minh and has since served in the foreign trade administration. Their shops and workshops became joint state-private enterprises in 1958–60, but some former owners still manage them and draw interest.

They quietly favour trade, private initiative in small industry and a gentler pace of socialist transformation, and value contacts with Hong Kong, Paris and overseas Chinese merchants. Politically harmless and carefully loyal, their leverage lies in commercial know-how the state still needs.

16.name: Khoan ho
16.text:
Khoan ho is the experiment in household contracting launched in 1966 in Vinh Phuc province by its party secretary Kim Ngoc, who let cooperative families farm assigned plots and keep the surplus above a fixed quota. Harvests rose sharply, but in 1968 the central leadership condemned the scheme as a deviation toward capitalism and ordered it stopped.

Its supporters, local cadres and peasants who saw it work, argue that rewarding the household is the only way to feed a nation at war and that rigid collectivization has failed the villages. They keep the practice alive in secret, and their leverage lies in results: wherever khoan ho is tolerated, the granaries fill.

17.name: Vuon quoc gia Cuc Phuong
17.text:
Cuc Phuong, the limestone forest where Ninh Binh, Hoa Binh and Thanh Hoa meet, was declared Vietnam's first protected forest in 1962, and Ho Chi Minh visited it in 1963, urging the people to love the forest as they love their homes. Its rangers, botanists and forestry scientists form the small nucleus of Northern conservation.

They campaign for reforestation, protection of wildlife and watersheds, and documentation of the damage done by American bombs and herbicides in the South and along the trail. Their influence is modest, resting on Ho's personal endorsement, the scientific institutes of Hanoi and the national tree-planting festival he founded.

18.name: Nhom Xet lai
18.text:
Nhom Xet lai is the name the party gives to the cadres arrested in 1967 in the so-called Revisionist Anti-Party Affair: officials, journalists and officers who favoured Soviet-style peaceful coexistence, economic reform and inner-party democracy. Its best-known figure, the philosopher Hoang Minh Chinh, has been held without trial since 1967, as has the veteran revolutionary Vu Dinh Huynh.

They argue for a socialist democracy closer to Moscow's reformers than to Mao's China, for a negotiated end to the war and for material incentives in the economy. Imprisoned or silenced, they still have sympathisers in the army, the press and the ministries, and their leverage lies in the quiet respect of cadres tired of purges.

20.name: Ba San sang
20.text:
Ba San sang, the 'Three Readies', is the patriotic mobilization launched in 1964 among Northern youth: ready to fight, ready to join the army, ready to go wherever the Fatherland calls. Run through the Working Youth Union, schools and cooperatives, it has become a mass movement of enlistment drives, rallies and village pledges that sends a constant stream of recruits south.

Its message is a plebeian nationalism that celebrates the soldier-peasant and the nation's thousand-year resistance to invaders, often more Vietnamese than Marxist in tone. It distrusts intellectuals and foreign advisers alike, and its leverage lies in the enthusiasm of rural youth and the families of the fallen.

21.name: Dai Viet Quoc dan Dang
21.text:
The Dai Viet Nationalist Party was founded in 1939 by Truong Tu Anh on a creed of 'national survivalism' inspired by European fascism, and was strong in the northern provinces until the Viet Minh destroyed it in 1946, the year Truong Tu Anh vanished. Its Northern leaders fled south in 1954, and on 1 January 1970 it exists in the North only as a clandestine memory hunted by the security police.

From Saigon its Northern branch dreams of a militarized, anti-communist Vietnam ruled by a nationalist elite, and sends agents and leaflets that rarely survive. Its leverage in the North is close to nil, but it gives the regime a ready enemy and the South a claim to speak for the lost provinces.

23.name: Nha Nguyen
23.text:
The Nguyen dynasty ruled from Hue until Emperor Bao Dai abdicated in August 1945, handing the imperial seal to the Viet Minh and briefly serving as 'Supreme Adviser' to Ho Chi Minh's government before leaving for Hong Kong. On 1 January 1970 he lives in France, and in the North the dynasty survives only in the memory of older mandarin families.

Monarchists imagine a neutral, reunified Vietnam under the crown, reconciling North and South above the parties. The party regards the dynasty as feudal and collaborationist, and its leverage inside the Democratic Republic is negligible, resting on nostalgia among Catholic and mandarin elders and exiles abroad.
